screens.heading: Why study real attacks

teacher.say: These are real, well-documented cases. Notice how ordinary each trick looks.

body: Real cases show that phishing is not a problem of careless people. Skilled staff at large, security-aware organisations have been caught, and the same few techniques appear each time.
In this module you will walk through three cases step by step. Tap each step to see how the attack unfolded.
screens.key_takeaway: Studying real attacks shows which simple checks would have stopped them.

screens.heading: Case 1: Fake supplier invoices (2013 to 2015)

teacher.say: Two huge technology companies paid these invoices. Tap each step to see how.

body: Google and Facebook were both reported to have paid fake invoices. The attacker did not break into any system. He simply asked for money in a believable way.

points.label: 1. Research
points.text: The fraudster identified a hardware manufacturer that the two companies genuinely bought equipment from.

points.label: 2. Bait
points.text: He set up a company with the same name as that supplier and sent convincing invoices, contracts and letters.

points.label: 3. Action
points.text: Finance teams paid the invoices into bank accounts he controlled.

points.label: 4. Payoff
points.text: Reports put the total above 100 million dollars. Most of it was later recovered.

example.title: What would have stopped it
example.text: Confirming new bank details and unusual payments with the real supplier by phone, using a number already on file.

screens.key_takeaway: Verify payment requests and changes of bank details through a separate channel you already know.

screens.heading: Case 2: The fake security alert (2016)

teacher.say: A single email, made to look like a routine warning, exposed thousands of messages.

body: In 2016 the chairman of a US presidential campaign received an email that looked like a security alert from his email provider, urging him to change his password.

points.label: 1. Research
points.text: The attacker targeted people close to a high-profile campaign.

points.label: 2. Bait
points.text: The email looked like a genuine security alert with a button to change the password. The link was shortened to hide where it led.

points.label: 3. Action
points.text: The link led to a fake sign-in page that captured the password.

points.label: 4. Payoff
points.text: The attacker read the mailbox, and thousands of emails were later published.

example.title: What would have stopped it
example.text: Going to the email provider's website directly instead of using the button, and protecting the account with a security key.

screens.key_takeaway: Never sign in through a link in an alert. Go to the service yourself.

screens.heading: Case 3: The phone call to IT (2020)

teacher.say: This one began with a phone call, not an email. Phishing is not only email.

body: In July 2020, attackers phoned employees of a major social media company while many were working from home. The callers claimed to be from the internal IT help desk.

points.label: 1. Research
points.text: The attackers learned who worked there and how remote staff reached internal systems.

points.label: 2. Bait
points.text: They phoned employees posing as IT support and sent them to a fake page built to look like the company's internal sign-in.

points.label: 3. Action
points.text: Employees entered their credentials on the fake page.

points.label: 4. Payoff
points.text: The attackers used internal tools to take over high-profile accounts and post a cryptocurrency scam.

example.title: What would have stopped it
example.text: Ending the call and phoning IT back on a number from the internal directory, plus sign-in methods that only work on the real website.

screens.key_takeaway: Never trust a caller who contacted you. Hang up and call back on a number you already know.

screens.heading: What the cases have in common

teacher.say: Three very different attacks, one pattern. Once you see it, you cannot unsee it.

body: Different channels, different targets, the same underlying method.

points.label: Borrowed trust
points.text: Every attack impersonated someone familiar: a supplier, a security team or the IT help desk.

points.label: A rushed human decision
points.text: Each one depended on a single person acting before checking.

points.label: Simple defences
points.text: Calling back on a known number, going to the site yourself, and using security keys or passkeys would each have broken the chain. Those sign-in methods only work on the real website, so they resist phishing even when a person is fooled.

points.label: Fast reporting
points.text: Quick reporting limits damage, because attackers often reuse the same trick on colleagues.

screens.key_takeaway: Attackers borrow trust. You win by verifying through a channel they do not control.
